title: What is type erasure in generics, and what does it make impossible (`new T()`, `instanceof List<String>`, generic arrays, overload by generic type), plus the PECS rule (`? extends` producer, `? super` consumer)?
shortTitle: What is type erasure in generics, what does it make impossible, and what is the PECS rule?
keyPoints: Type erasure removes generic type information after compile-time checking, replacing type parameters with their bounds or Object.
At runtime List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class (raw List), which is the single fact explaining every restriction.
new T(), instanceof List<String>, generic arrays like new T[], and generic-only overloads are impossible after erasure.
The standard workaround for new T() is passing a Class<T> token and constructing reflectively.
PECS means Producer Extends Consumer Super: use ? extends T to read and ? super T to write.
Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) is the canonical PECS example.
Erasure is why generics have zero runtime cost and why you sometimes see unchecked-cast warnings.

s1_definition.oneliner: Type erasure deletes generic types at runtime so new T, instanceof on a parameterized type, generic arrays, and generic-only overloads are impossible, and PECS says read with extends and write with super.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Type erasure** – The compiler's process of removing generic type information after compile-time checking, replacing type parameters with their bounds or `Object`, and inserting casts.
- **Runtime consequence** – `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same class at runtime (raw `List`), so the JVM has no knowledge of the element type.
- **Impossible operations** – `new T()`, `instanceof List<String>`, `new T[]`, and overloading by generic type argument all fail because of erasure.
- **Class token workaround** – Pass a `Class<T>` to recover type information at runtime, e.g., `clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()`.
- **PECS** – Producer Extends, Consumer Super: use `? extends T` when reading from a structure and `? super T` when writing into one.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India stamps every form with a label like "this box only accepts savings-account records" while the clerk checks the forms (compile time). But once the forms are filed, the label is peeled off and every box just says "records" (runtime erasure). So later you cannot ask a filed box "were you originally the savings-only box?" because the label is gone. PECS is the handling rule: if you are reading records out of a box, label it "produces account records" so you can read safely; if you are putting records in, label it "accepts accounts or any parent type" so writes are valid.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Type erasure is the compiler's process of using generic type information to check code at compile time and then removing it, replacing each type parameter with its bound or Object and inserting casts. The practical consequence is that at runtime a List<String> and a List<Integer> are the same class, plain List, because the element type is gone. So generics are a compile-time safety feature with zero runtime cost.

That one fact makes several things impossible. new T() fails because at runtime T is erased and the JVM does not know which constructor to call, so the workaround is passing a Class<T> token. instanceof on a parameterized type like List<String> fails because the runtime only sees raw List. Generic arrays like new T[] conflict with arrays' reified store checks. And overloading by generic type argument clashes because both methods have the same raw signature.

PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super) is the rule for wildcard bounds. A List<? extends T> is a producer: you can safely read every element as T but cannot add. A List<? super T> is a consumer: you can safely add T values but when reading you only get Object back. If a parameter is a source you read from, use extends. If it is a sink you write into, use super. If you both read and write, use an exact T.

In banking work at National Bank of India a generic repository could not use new T(), so it took a Class token and created instances reflectively. A reporting utility summed balances over a List<? extends Account> so it could accept a list of SavingsAccount and read every element as Account. An onboarding utility added savings records into a List<? super SavingsAccount> so it could write into a list typed to Account.

Remember one sentence: type erasure removes generic types at runtime making new T() and instanceof on parameterized types impossible, and PECS says use extends to read and super to write.
